title: How 'Spider-Noir' VFX Team Stuck to a 'Dogmatic' Plan to Pull Off Complex Sequences
summary: A show like 'Spider-Noir' requires technical filmmaking at the highest level from every department. In addition to the star power of Nicolas Cage, the stakes were raised by the intricacy of comic book-inspired sequences. Many scenes combined practical stunts with post-production effects, which meant intense preparation and frequent communication were non-negotiable. During IndieWire's Emmy season Craft Roundtables, 'Spider-Noir' VFX supervisor Hnedel Maximore broke down his process. He explained that there was little room for improvisation because of the need for precise timing. The VFX department had to previsualize key sequences and precisely communicate their needs to the stunt team, then stick to the plan all the way through editing. 'On 'Spider-Noir,' we had a lot of technical, timing things that are highly dependent on stunts and special effects and all of the departments playing well together,' Maximore said. 'We stayed true to a lot of the sequences that we planned and prevized and shot for. And you have to be dogmatic about it because otherwise you blow your budget, or you lose the tone of the show.' Dogmatic means adhering strictly to a set of principles. The show, set in 1930s New York, follows Ben Reilly (Cage), a private investigator grappling with his past as the city's only superhero. The eight-episode first season is now streaming on Prime Video.
why_it_matters: This peek behind the camera reveals that the most exciting shows aren’t just magic — they are built on extreme discipline and teamwork. For young people interested in filmmaking, gaming, or any creative tech, it proves that the wildest ideas often need the strictest planning to work.

background_read: 'Spider-Noir' is a Prime Video (Amazon's streaming service) series based on Marvel's darker Spider-Man Noir comics, which reimagine the hero in a stylish, shadowy 1930s setting.

Nicolas Cage, the Oscar-winning actor known for his intense and unusual performances, stars as Ben Reilly, a private investigator who used to be the city's only superhero — a very different take from the teenaged Peter Parker most fans know.

Visual effects (VFX) have become essential to modern television, and previsualization — making rough animated storyboards — was pioneered by filmmakers like George Lucas to plan complex action safely and within budget.

Sticking to a 'dogmatic' plan is unusual in creative projects where changes often happen on set, but it’s increasingly common in VFX-heavy productions because even small deviations can cause expensive chain reactions in post-production.

perspectives.description: Fans get visually impressive, thrilling sequences that feel coherent and stylish because everything was planned. The dogmatic method ensures the final product matches the original vision, avoiding messy last-minute fixes.

Some directors and actors argue that too much pre-planning leaves no room for happy accidents or raw, in-the-moment performances, potentially making scenes feel mechanically perfect but emotionally cold.

As TV budgets and expectations grow, productions are forced to adopt film-like VFX pipelines. This industrial approach isn't new — it mirrors how big movies have worked for decades — but it does raise the barrier for more experimental, improvised storytelling on this scale.

Real-time rendering and virtual production tools are starting to let filmmakers see VFX while shooting, which could combine the dogmatic planning with more on-set flexibility. Future shows might be able to plan tightly and still improvise without breaking the bank.
